findings: The candidate preserves the recovered source facts: input characters are 1-9, the whole string is partitioned contiguously into at least three numbers, adjacent terms satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence, and the result is Boolean.

The source does not preserve a maximum input length or integer width. Choosing BigInteger is therefore presented as an implementation strategy that avoids inventing a fixed-width overflow boundary rather than as an original problem requirement.

Once the first two cuts are fixed, every later term is uniquely determined by addition. The candidate correctly narrows the search to the genuinely free decisions and then performs deterministic suffix matching.

The sufficiency argument requires complete input consumption and at least one generated sum, while the completeness argument follows because any valid solution has a first-cut/second-cut pair that the outer enumeration visits.
The implementation validates the source-domain alphabet instead of silently accepting zero or unrelated characters; null and out-of-domain behavior are clearly labelled as candidate API choices.

The executable fixture passes eight fixed cases including an arbitrary-precision value beyond long range and 5000 deterministic randomized source-domain strings against a structurally different recursive all-partitions oracle.
The candidate does not import LeetCode size bounds, leading-zero rules outside the source domain, fixed integer limits, or fabricated production history.

The complexity discussion explicitly distinguishes the O(L^2) free split choices from suffix scanning and arbitrary-precision digit costs instead of claiming a stronger source-required bound. Human approval remains a separate promotion gate.
